Why Boston generates MT demand

New England's inspection work runs through Boston — gas and nuclear generation support, aerospace and defence suppliers along the 128 corridor, marine work across the harbour and shipyards, and the LNG import terminal at Everett.

Turbine components, boiler headers and structural welds take MT during outages — surface cracking at stub welds and attachment details is a known header mechanism.

Landing gear and engine components in martensitic steels are magnetic particle territory — high-strength parts where grinding cracks and fatigue must be found at overhaul.

In-process MT on fit-ups, tack repairs and completed structural welds catches surface defects while rework is cheap.

Class surveys call MT on hatch corners, crane pedestals, rudder horns and other fatigue-prone details, where the finding decides steel renewal scope.

What typically gets examined

In practice that means MT work across power plant pressure parts, aerospace and defence components, harbour and terminal infrastructure, and LNG import equipment — with scope set by the damage mechanisms each asset actually runs, not by a standard menu.

Certification and acceptance in Boston

Massachusetts statutory equipment follows NBIC with state boiler enforcement; defence and aerospace suppliers carry NAS 410 personnel requirements and ITAR-controlled documentation, which shapes who can even see the work.

Examinations themselves are performed to ASME Section V Article 7, ASTM E709 and E1444, and the ISO 9934 series, with acceptance from the governing construction code. The evidence chain — technician certification current on the day, instrument and reference block calibration, and the procedure revision in force — travels with every report, because that bundle is what an audit actually checks.
